The ideaOne sentence the whole design follows

The analyst opens an incident that is already investigated

Questions, not data types

The screen follows what the analyst asks: What happened? What was done? What do you need from me?

The agent writes the screen

There is no chat panel waiting for a question. The agent’s work is the content.

The new risk is over-trust

The danger is to believe the agent when it is wrong. So every claim shows its evidence.

The processHow I used AI

Seven steps, with AI at every one

StepWith AIMy decision
1. Read the briefRead it together, line by lineThe main question: how to show work the analyst did not do
2. Study what existsSummarized public sources on Cortex and four other toolsA summary, a chat and an approve button are already the baseline
3. Find the ideaOffered several framings“A review, not a workbench”
4. Write a scenarioWrote a realistic incident and its dataKept the story with a real trade-off
5. Draw conceptsDrew four directions on the same incidentChose one, kept one idea from each of the others
6. Attack the conceptListed what every candidate would also bringWhat not to present as a new idea
7. BuildWrote the prototype codeReviewed, adjusted and deployed it

The pathFrom four directions to one

Four concepts, one choice

AVersions

Shows what was ruled out, but it is heavy for most incidents.

BReview

Clear ownership, but too much ceremony for a simple incident.

CRace

Shows consequences well, but a timeline cannot hold the whole story.

DCase file

Chosen. The fastest to read. Trust is part of the text itself.

One idea kept from each of the others

  • From Review: options with their cost, not yes or no.
  • From Race: a timeline with a forecast, under the story.
  • From Versions: what was ruled out, inside the trace.

The final screenWhat is where

123456
  1. 1The verdict. What happened, is it contained, what is needed.
  2. 2The story. What the agent found, as claims with evidence.
  3. 3The race. Attacker against response, with a forecast.
  4. 4The decision. The one thing that needs a person. The key component.
  5. 5Done without you. Reversible steps, each with Undo.
  6. 6Checked, and not known. What was ruled out, and the blind spots.

The brief “help analysts quickly understand what happened and explore relevant information”

Parts 1 and 2The verdict and the story

Understand in ten seconds

  1. 1One line answers three questions before any scroll.
  2. 2The attacker’s clock. A forecast of the next move, not an SLA timer.
  3. 337 alerts become a few sentences. Each one is a claim.
  4. 4The underline shows how sure the agent is: observed, inferred, unknown, or confirmed by a person.
  5. 5Click a claim and its evidence opens beside it.

The agent’s work, made visible

  1. 1Three lanes: the attacker, the agents, the people.
  2. 2Time stretches where things move fast. Machines act in seconds.
  3. 3Right of “now”: the forecast, and the response the agent has ready.
  4. 4Checked and clear. What the agent ruled out.
  5. 5What I don’t know. Blind spots, said out loud.

The brief “how the agent’s work is reflected back to the analyst”

Part 4The key component: the decision card

123456

The moment the agent asks for a decision

  1. 1One request, starting with a verb.
  2. 2The attacker’s clock. The cost of waiting.
  3. 3Three options, not yes or no. One is recommended.
  4. 4Consequences before the click: what it stops, what it breaks, how to recover.
  5. 5Hold to approve. The risky option needs a hold. The safe one needs one click.
  6. 6A fallback if nobody answers.

The brief “A moment where the agent asks the analyst for input or approval”

Part 4The decision card in depth

One card, five states

Needs you

The request, the options and the cost.

Running

The card does not close. It shows each step.

Done

A receipt, and an offer to make it a rule next time.

Declined

One tap for the reason. The agent says what it does instead.

No answer

The agent takes the small safe step and calls the backup.

BehaviorThe screen over time

The screen changes with the incident

02:21Opened

The decision is on top. The story is already written.

02:22Decided

The band turns green. A new sentence appears in the story.

02:25Contained

“I don’t know” becomes a fact. The old text stays crossed out.

09:00Morning

The same screen is now a report. Five drafts wait for a signature.

The brief “Show the magic and the automations”

More viewsTwo situations around the main screen

When the agent is wrong

The analyst disputes a sentence. The agent rewrites it, keeps the old text visible, and fixes what follows.

How the agent got here

The trace shows the questions the agent asked itself, not a log. 8 of 61 steps by default.

Try it: five things to do in the prototype

by Igor Kaufman

Try it yourself

  1. 1Click any underlined sentence. Its evidence opens beside it.
  2. 2Hold “Hold to approve”. Or pick another option, or decline.
  3. 3Wait a few seconds. The unknown becomes a fact.
  4. 4Dispute the sentence “No other endpoint ran the package”.
  5. 5Jump in time with the buttons at the top of the page.
Open the prototype incident-prototype-inky.vercel.app

Good to know

  • The What to try button in the site’s header lists these steps too.
  • The scenario, the names and the numbers are invented.
  • The command bar runs five fixed commands.
  • It is built for a desktop screen first.

What I would test next

  • How fast analysts reach the right verdict.
  • How often they dispute a claim.
  • A planted error: do they catch one false sentence?
